strengths: The paper identifies an important and timely failure mode for time-series foundation models in scientific forecasting: strong apparent zero-shot performance can arise from copying repeated motifs rather than learning physically meaningful representations.

The proposed context-parroting baseline is simple, interpretable, computationally cheap, and empirically strong on the dysts chaotic-systems benchmark, making it potentially useful as a sanity-check baseline for future work.

The evaluation covers a reasonably broad set of 135 low-dimensional chaotic systems, multiple context lengths, several modern time-series foundation models, and multiple error metrics in the appendix.

The connection to induction heads, kernel regression, delay embeddings, and classical nonlinear forecasting is conceptually interesting and helps position the mechanism relative to both transformer behavior and dynamical-systems theory.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited because the method is essentially nearest-neighbor forecasting in delay-embedding space, closely related to simplex projection, S-map methods, analog forecasting, and nonparametric time-series regression. The paper acknowledges these links but still frames the baseline as more novel than it may be.

The experimental comparison is incomplete for the central claims. The paper compares against foundation models but not against strong classical dynamical-systems baselines such as simplex projection, S-map variants, analog ensemble methods, reservoir computing, or tuned kNN/kernel forecasters. This makes it hard to know whether context parroting is the right baseline or just one representative of a known family.

The claims about foundation models failing to learn meaningful physics are stronger than the evidence. Poor performance on univariate forecasts of low-dimensional deterministic chaotic systems does not by itself establish a lack of physical representations, especially without probing representations, fine-tuning, multivariate inputs, or domain-matched evaluation.

The computational-cost comparison is potentially unfair or at least underspecified: all model inference is run on CPUs, while these foundation models are typically deployed on accelerators. The six-order-of-magnitude claim may still be directionally true, but the exact comparison needs hardware-normalized or deployment-relevant reporting.

The evaluation scope is narrow relative to the broad conclusions. The benchmark consists of stationary, autonomous, low-dimensional chaotic ODE systems with long clean simulated trajectories. The results may not transfer to noisy, nonstationary, multivariate, partially observed, irregularly sampled, or real scientific time series.

The scaling-law analysis is suggestive but not fully convincing. The empirical correlation between inverse scaling coefficient and correlation dimension is modest, the estimation procedure is noisy, and the theoretical derivation glosses over temporal dependence, finite-sample effects, embedding dimension choices, and the distinction between nearest-neighbor distance scaling and forecast-error scaling.

Important reproducibility details are missing or underdeveloped, including model preprocessing/normalization, exact decoding settings for probabilistic models such as Chronos, implementation details for context parroting, hyperparameter choices, confidence intervals for main performance curves, and whether code/data splits are released.

Some statements are overgeneralized, such as suggesting infinite context yields infinite accuracy for any stationary deterministic system, or that current time-series foundation models broadly fail as general-purpose forecasters. These claims need sharper qualifications.

strengths: The paper asks a timely and relevant question: whether time-series foundation models genuinely learn useful physical structure when used zero-shot on chaotic dynamical systems.
weaknesses: The central method is essentially nearest-neighbor delay-embedding forecasting, closely related to classical nonlinear forecasting methods such as simplex projection and S-map. The paper acknowledges this but does not convincingly establish novelty beyond repackaging it as "context parroting."

The empirical evaluation is too narrow for the breadth of the claims. Results are almost entirely on low-dimensional deterministic chaotic systems from dysts, yet the paper makes broad statements about foundation models for scientific machine learning and time-series forecasting.

Key baselines are missing or underdeveloped. A fair study should compare against classical nearest-neighbor, simplex projection, S-map, reservoir computing, and simple autoregressive/statistical baselines under matched tuning and compute, not only against foundation models.

The benchmark setup may favor copying methods: long context windows are sampled from the same trajectory/distribution as the forecast target, and the task is deterministic, stationary, and low-dimensional. This makes nearest-neighbor recurrence unusually strong and does not demonstrate general zero-shot forecasting ability.

Claims that foundation models "fail to develop meaningful representations of the underlying physics" are not adequately supported. Worse forecasting than a nearest-neighbor baseline on this benchmark does not imply absence of physical representations or mechanisms.

The inference-cost comparison is not very meaningful as presented. Running large foundation models on CPU and comparing wall-clock time to a simple nearest-neighbor routine exaggerates the practical gap and does not control for implementation, hardware, batching, or intended deployment.

The theoretical contribution is weak relative to the claims. Much of the kernel-regression and ergodic-invariant discussion appears standard, and the scaling-law connection is only loosely supported empirically; the reported correlation between inverse scaling coefficient and correlation dimension is modest.

The paper does not sufficiently probe failure modes of context parroting, such as noisy observations, partial observability beyond simple univariate forecasts, nonstationarity, distribution shift, irregular sampling, stochastic dynamics, or systems where recurrence in the context is rare.

Some conclusions are overstated. The results support context parroting as a useful baseline for a particular chaotic-system benchmark, but not as evidence that current time-series foundation models are generally uninformative or that benchmark performance is largely gamed by repetition.

strengths: Clear and timely central message: a very simple context-copying/nearest-neighbor baseline can outperform current time-series foundation models on chaotic dynamical-system forecasting. This is useful and potentially field-shaping for SciML benchmarking.

The empirical setup is reasonably broad within its chosen domain, using 135 systems from dysts, multiple model families (Chronos, Chronos-Bolt, TimesFM, TimeMoE), multiple context lengths, and several metrics including sMAPE, VPT, MSE, and MAE.
The paper is well written and easy to follow. The figures communicate the main phenomena clearly, especially the dependence on context length and the comparison to foundation models.
The connection to classical nonlinear forecasting, induction-head-like copying, and in-context scaling laws gives the work more conceptual value than a pure benchmark note.

The result is practically important: it argues convincingly that future zero-shot time-series foundation-model papers should include simple copying/nearest-neighbor baselines before claiming emergent physical reasoning.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat limited because context parroting is essentially nearest-neighbor delay embedding, closely related to simplex projection, S-map, empirical dynamic modeling, and analog forecasting. The paper acknowledges these links, but the positioning could still overstate the method’s conceptual originality.

The claim that foundation models fail to develop meaningful physical representations is stronger than the evidence. The experiments show underperformance on this benchmark, but do not provide direct representation analysis or rule out other mechanisms, preprocessing disadvantages, or model-specific usage issues.

The evaluation is narrow despite using many systems: all main tests are low-dimensional, deterministic, stationary chaotic ODE systems, with univariate forecasts per dimension. This does not establish the baseline as broadly tough-to-beat for realistic scientific forecasting with noise, partial observability, irregular sampling, multivariate coupling, PDEs, weather-like fields, or nonstationarity.

Important baselines are missing or underdeveloped. Since the proposed method is closely tied to classical nonlinear forecasting, direct comparisons to optimized simplex projection, S-map/EDM, kNN analog forecasting, reservoir methods, and simple persistence/seasonal baselines would make the empirical case much stronger.

Some experimental details are underspecified for reproducibility, including exact preprocessing/normalization, model prompting/tokenization settings, whether foundation models were used in their recommended modes, hardware/runtime measurement details, and whether code will be released.

The scaling-law argument is interesting but not fully convincing. The empirical correlation between inverse scaling coefficient and correlation dimension is moderate, noisy, and based on a particular D and one-step error; the theory relies on idealized assumptions that are not carefully reconciled with finite-context, finite-sample practice.

The cost comparison may be somewhat misleading because all inference is performed on CPUs, whereas large foundation models are normally deployed with optimized GPU batching. The qualitative cost advantage likely remains, but the reported six-order gap should be interpreted cautiously.

Aggregation over systems, dimensions, and initial conditions hides heterogeneity. The paper would benefit from per-system breakdowns, uncertainty intervals on primary metrics, significance testing, and analysis of cases where Chronos beats parroting at short context lengths.

strengths: Clear and timely central message: a very simple context-copying nearest-neighbor baseline can outperform several prominent time-series foundation models on zero-shot forecasting of dynamical systems, which is useful and potentially impactful for SciML benchmarking.

The empirical evaluation is fairly broad for the main claim: 135 low-dimensional chaotic systems, multiple metrics, several context lengths, noise and sampling-rate checks, and additional tasks spanning fluid dynamics, ECG, electronic circuits, and Kuramoto oscillators.
The paper is well written and connects the empirical phenomenon to relevant ideas from Takens embeddings, nonlinear forecasting, induction heads, and in-context scaling laws.
The analysis of failure modes, especially regression to the mean for some foundation models and saturation with context length, is informative and could guide better model and benchmark design.
The proposed baseline is simple, cheap, and easy to understand, making it a practically valuable diagnostic even if not conceptually new.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited because the method is essentially nearest-neighbor forecasting in delay-embedded space, closely related to simplex projection, S-map, and Farmer-Sidorowich methods. These are discussed but not experimentally included as baselines, which is a major omission for a paper framed around a tough-to-beat SciML baseline.

The evaluation focuses on foundation models but does not compare against strong classical nonlinear time-series baselines under the same conditions. This weakens claims about context parroting as a broadly superior or especially informative forecasting strategy.

The theoretical contribution is suggestive but not fully convincing. The invariant-preservation proposition relies on idealized limits and ergodicity assumptions, and the scaling-law evidence linking inverse scaling coefficient to correlation dimension is only moderately correlated, so the theory feels more explanatory than rigorously validated.

Some comparisons may be sensitive to implementation and evaluation choices: univariate independent forecasting of multivariate systems, fixed embedding dimension for parroting, model-specific context limits, CPU-only timing, and unclear hyperparameter or preprocessing details for all foundation models.

Reproducibility appears incomplete: the manuscript does not provide an explicit code/data release link or enough implementation detail to fully reproduce all model calls, runtime measurements, and benchmark pipelines.

The paper occasionally overstates implications, such as suggesting that foundation models do not fully utilize context data, when the evidence may instead reflect mismatch between model training objectives, inference settings, tokenization, and chaotic-system benchmarks.

strengths: The paper asks a relevant and timely question: whether current time-series foundation models actually exploit context well for scientific dynamical forecasting.
The proposed context-parroting baseline is simple, easy to understand, computationally cheap, and empirically useful as a sanity-check baseline.

The empirical scope is broader than a single toy system: the paper evaluates 135 low-dimensional chaotic systems and includes additional SciML-style tasks such as ECG, electronic circuits, Kuramoto oscillators, and von Karman flow.

The paper reports multiple metrics and some robustness checks over noise, sampling granularity, context length, and embedding dimension, which helps establish that the observed effect is not purely metric-specific.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. Context parroting is essentially delay-coordinate nearest-neighbor forecasting, closely related to classical nonlinear time-series methods such as simplex projection, S-map, and Farmer-Sidorowich local models. The paper acknowledges these links but does not compare against these stronger and more relevant classical baselines, which substantially weakens the contribution.

The central empirical comparison is incomplete. Showing that a nearest-neighbor baseline beats several foundation models is useful, but without comparisons to established nonparametric dynamical forecasting methods, reservoir methods, local linear models, and simple kNN variants, it is hard to know whether the paper contributes more than a repackaged known baseline.

Several claims about foundation models using parroting are under-supported. The paper gives examples and cites prior observations, but does not provide mechanistic evidence, attention/circuit analysis, or systematic diagnostics showing that the evaluated models implement the proposed algorithm.

The theoretical component is overstated. The claimed scaling relation between context length and attractor dimension is mostly heuristic, the empirical correlation in the appendix is only moderate, and the invariant-preservation proposition is close to a generic ergodic/nearest-neighbor consistency observation rather than a strong new result about foundation models.

The evaluation may favor the proposed method in ways that are not fully addressed: context parroting can use arbitrarily long contexts while model context windows are fixed, inference-cost comparisons are CPU-only and may not reflect optimized deployment, and model-specific prompting, normalization, decoding, or probabilistic sampling choices are not deeply analyzed.

The broader SciML experiments are summarized in small tables with limited methodological detail, making it difficult to assess statistical reliability, dataset leakage risks, horizon choices, preprocessing, and whether each model was evaluated under its recommended settings.

The discussion sometimes makes claims that are stronger than the evidence, including broad statements about time-series foundation models not fully utilizing context and speculative connections to induction heads and language-model scaling laws.

Reproducibility is not fully convincing from the manuscript alone: implementation details for the foundation models, exact hyperparameters, seeds, preprocessing, and code availability are not sufficiently specified for a high-confidence reproduction.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and timely failure mode of time-series foundation models for scientific forecasting: several large pretrained models can be outperformed by a very simple context-copying nearest-neighbor baseline on chaotic and oscillatory systems.

The empirical study is broad and mostly convincing: it covers 135 low-dimensional chaotic systems, multiple metrics including short-horizon error and attractor-level statistics, several recent foundation models, context-length sweeps, noise and sampling-rate sensitivity, and additional SciML datasets including ECG, electronic circuits, Kuramoto oscillators, and fluid dynamics.

The paper is unusually interpretable for this area. The framing of context parroting as a simple in-context mechanism related to induction heads, kernel regression, Takens-style delay embeddings, and classical nonlinear forecasting is clear and useful.

The results are practically significant: the baseline is not only more accurate in many tested settings but also orders of magnitude cheaper at inference, making it a valuable diagnostic benchmark for future time-series foundation models.

The writing is clear, the figures and tables support the main story, and the authors are appropriately careful in the conclusion that context parroting is primarily a baseline and diagnostic tool rather than a full replacement for foundation models.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat limited because the proposed method is essentially a nearest-neighbor delay-embedding forecaster, closely related to classical methods such as simplex projection, S-map, and Farmer-Sidorowich forecasting. The paper discusses these links but does not empirically compare against these classical nonlinear forecasting baselines, which is a notable omission given the central claim.

The evaluation is strongest against time-series foundation models, but weaker as a general SciML forecasting study. It would be important to include strong non-foundation zero-shot or training-free baselines, local linear models, kNN variants, adaptive embedding choices, and simple seasonal/recurrence baselines to clarify whether the contribution is specifically about foundation-model benchmarking or about forecasting more broadly.

Some comparisons may favor parroting structurally: parroting can use arbitrarily long context, while several foundation models have fixed context windows; all models are evaluated with univariate independent forecasts even for multivariate systems; and CPU inference timing may not reflect optimized or intended deployment of foundation models.

The theoretical component is insightful but not fully satisfying. The invariant-preservation result is largely asymptotic and close to an ergodic/kNN consistency argument, while the claimed link between scaling exponent and attractor dimension is supported empirically only moderately, with a reported Spearman correlation around 0.51.

The paper could better separate cases where parroting succeeds because the task contains recurring motifs from cases requiring genuine extrapolation, nonstationarity handling, or causal/physical abstraction. Such stress tests would strengthen the claim that the benchmark reveals limitations of foundation models rather than primarily rewarding recurrence lookup.

Reproducibility details are incomplete from the manuscript alone: implementation choices for each foundation model, normalization, batching, hardware, random seeds, hyperparameters for parroting, and code/data release are not described in enough detail to fully audit the reported results.

strengths: Clear and useful central message: a very simple nearest-neighbor/context-copying baseline is highly competitive with, and often better than, current time-series foundation models on chaotic forecasting tasks.

Empirical evaluation is broader than many papers in this area, covering 135 low-dimensional chaotic systems plus turbulence, ECG, circuits, and Kuramoto-style systems, with several modern foundation-model baselines.

The paper is well motivated and clearly written, with intuitive figures and a helpful connection between context parroting, induction-head-style copying, delay embeddings, and classical nonlinear forecasting.

The work has practical benchmark value: it argues convincingly that future SciML/time-series foundation models should be compared against simple context-reuse baselines before making claims about learned physical understanding.
Multiple metrics are considered, including short-horizon forecast error and longer-horizon attractor/spectral properties, which is appropriate for chaotic systems.
weaknesses: The core algorithm is essentially nearest-neighbor delay-coordinate forecasting and is closely related to simplex projection, S-map methods, and classical nonlinear time-series methods; the novelty is more in positioning and benchmarking than in the method itself.

The theoretical claims are somewhat overstated. The derivation linking scaling exponents to inverse correlation dimension is plausible, but relies on strong assumptions about ergodicity, sampling, finite-context nearest-neighbor behavior, and the relation between motif distance and forecast error. The invariant-preservation argument is also not fully rigorous for finite horizons or periodic parroted rollouts.

Some comparisons may favor parroting structurally: the task gives a context from the same system and trajectory distribution, while several foundation models have fixed context limits, tokenization/normalization assumptions, or were not designed specifically for chaotic physical systems.

The evaluation would be stronger with more detailed reproducibility information, including exact model versions/checkpoints, preprocessing choices, inference settings, hardware/runtime details, code release, and hyperparameter selection protocol for embedding dimension and baselines.

The paper does not fully disentangle when foundation models genuinely parrot from when the hand-coded parrot baseline simply exploits recurrence in deterministic systems. Stronger mechanistic evidence inside model attention or outputs would support the induction-head interpretation.
The broader SciML tables show parroting is often top-three but not uniformly best; the text occasionally phrases the conclusions more strongly than these mixed results justify.

Classical nonlinear forecasting baselines are relegated mostly to the appendix, despite being the closest methodological competitors. More prominent and carefully tuned comparisons to kNN, simplex, S-map, Farmer-Sidorowich/local linear methods, and reservoir approaches would better calibrate the contribution.

strengths: The paper identifies a simple and important baseline for zero-shot forecasting of dynamical systems: nearest-neighbor/context-copying over the available trajectory. This is a useful reminder that strong-looking foundation-model results can be explained by simple in-context reuse rather than learned physics.

The empirical evaluation is broader than many baseline papers: it includes multiple time-series foundation models, DynaMix, many low-dimensional chaotic systems from dysts, several metrics, and additional tasks such as ECG, circuits, turbulence, and Kuramoto oscillators.
The paper is generally clear and easy to follow, with helpful figures illustrating the context-parroting mechanism and common failure modes such as regression to the mean.
The connection to classical nonlinear forecasting, induction-head-like copying, and attractor-dimension scaling is intellectually interesting, even if not fully convincing as presented.
weaknesses: The core method is essentially a nearest-neighbor delay-embedding baseline, closely related to classical nonlinear forecasting methods such as simplex projection, S-map, and Farmer-Sidorowich. The novelty is therefore limited, and the paper sometimes presents the baseline as more conceptually new than it is.

The central interpretive claim that foundation models forecast by parroting is not strongly established. The evidence is mostly behavioral and anecdotal, especially for Chronos, without mechanistic analysis, controlled interventions, or systematic attribution showing that the models actually implement the proposed algorithm.

The evaluation may favor context parroting in ways that weaken the conclusions. The main benchmark uses stationary deterministic systems with repeated motifs, univariate independent forecasting, and context-only reconstruction metrics, which are exactly the regime where nearest-neighbor copying should excel. This does not by itself show broad failure of time-series foundation models or lack of learned dynamics.

Classical baselines are under-emphasized and possibly underdeveloped. Simplex projection and AutoARIMA appear mainly in the appendix, and stronger local nonlinear methods, tuned kNN variants, S-map/local linear models, reservoir computing, or task-specific SciML baselines are not given a central, carefully tuned comparison.

The comparison to foundation models is not always apples-to-apples. Some models have fixed context limits, different training objectives, different probabilistic outputs, and may require model-specific preprocessing or prompting choices. The paper does not provide enough detail to know whether each foundation model was used optimally.

The broader SciML results are mixed and thinly described. In the additional tasks, parroting is not consistently best, and some claims are softened to ranking in the top three. Dataset construction, splits, preprocessing, dimensionality handling, and statistical significance are insufficiently detailed for such broad claims.

The theoretical section is suggestive but informal. The scaling-law argument relies on strong assumptions about ergodicity, nearest-neighbor distances, embedding dimension, and the relation between motif distance and forecast error. It does not rigorously explain neural scaling laws for LLMs or foundation models, only a similar scaling behavior for the proposed baseline.

The invariant-property discussion is potentially misleading. Since context parroting produces periodic continuations, claims about preserving chaotic invariants require careful finite-sample qualification. The paper acknowledges this but still leans on invariant metrics that may be gamed by copying long observed segments.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript: the reproducibility statement says code and benchmarks are available at, but no URL or artifact is provided in the extracted text. Important implementation details for baselines and model inference are also sparse.

Overall, the paper has a useful message and some convincing empirical observations, but the contribution is closer to a cautionary baseline study than a strong top-tier conference paper. The claims about foundation-model mechanisms and broad SciML implications are stronger than the evidence supports.

strengths: Clear and timely contribution: the paper identifies context parroting as a simple, interpretable, and computationally cheap baseline that exposes meaningful limitations of current time-series foundation models on scientific forecasting tasks.

The empirical evaluation is broad for the main claim, covering 135 low-dimensional chaotic systems and additional SciML settings including turbulence, ECG, electronic circuits, and Kuramoto oscillators.
The comparison set is strong and relevant, including Chronos, Chronos-Bolt, TimesFM, Time-MoE, Moirai, DynaMix, and appendix comparisons to classical methods such as simplex projection and AutoARIMA.

The paper goes beyond short-horizon point error by evaluating attractor KL divergence, power spectra, fractal dimension, Lyapunov-related quantities, noise robustness, sampling-rate robustness, and context-length scaling.

The connection to nearest-neighbor forecasting, induction-head-like copying, and in-context scaling laws is conceptually useful and helps explain why simple copying strategies can look surprisingly strong in dynamical forecasting benchmarks.
The writing is generally clear, the algorithm is easy to understand, and the main message is likely to influence benchmark design for scientific time-series foundation models.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat limited because context parroting is very close to classical nearest-neighbor, delay-embedding, simplex projection, and Nadaraya-Watson forecasting. The paper positions this well in the appendix, but the main contribution is more a reframing and benchmark lesson than a fundamentally new method.

Some claims about foundation models using parroting are stronger than the evidence provided. Chronos is shown with a compelling example, but the paper does not provide systematic mechanistic evidence that the evaluated foundation models implement parroting or induction-head-like circuits.

The evaluation favors stationary deterministic or near-deterministic systems where recurrence in the context is expected to be highly informative. This is appropriate for the stated SciML scope, but limits the generality of conclusions about time-series foundation models more broadly.

The fairness of some comparisons could be sharpened. Foundation models have fixed context limits, different training objectives, and are evaluated mostly as univariate independent forecasters; it is not always clear whether model-specific preprocessing, sampling choices, or hyperparameters are fully optimized.

The real-world and high-dimensional task section is promising but relatively compressed. More details on train/test splits, preprocessing, dimensional projections, statistical significance, and failure cases would make the broader claims more convincing.

The theoretical scaling argument is insightful but somewhat informal. The relation between finite-context forecast error, nearest-neighbor distance, embedding dimension, sampling density, and correlation dimension relies on assumptions that are not fully formalized or stress-tested.

The reproducibility statement appears incomplete: it says code and benchmarks are available at a location, but the actual URL or artifact identifier is missing in the manuscript text I inspected. This should be fixed before publication.
